title: Encodings and Node Architecture: Lessons from the Fault-Tolerant Distributed Transversal Fanout
abstract: An encoding choice specifies the quantum error-correcting code used to encode logical qubits at a given node. Different encoding choices may differ in the number of physical qubits, the number of encoded logical qubits, the code distance, and the available fault-tolerant operations. We study different encodings for a distributed transversal fanout operation and look at its implications on node architecture. Our experiments suggest that an encoding with higher distance, even if requiring more ebits, can yield a lower logical error rate for distributed operations, and that ``upgrading'' an encoding prior to distributed operations and having a cache, as part of node architecture, for qubits can be useful for distributed operations.
summary: This work analyzes the trade-offs between quantum error-correcting code encodings when performing complex distributed operations like fanout. It demonstrates that prioritizing higher code distance, even at the cost of more physical qubits, can significantly lower the logical error rate. The authors also propose architectural enhancements, such as encoding upgrading and caching, to boost fault tolerance in distributed quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the choice of quantum error-correcting code encoding impacts the performance of fault-tolerant distributed transversal fanout operations in quantum computing.
main_result: Higher code distance encodings can achieve lower logical error rates for distributed operations, even if they require more physical qubits, and implementing node caching can further improve performance.
method: The study uses theoretical comparison and simulation via the Transversal Multiple Code Block Simulator (TMCBS) library to compare different encoding strategies and fanout implementations.
model_or_system: The model is a distributed quantum computing architecture involving multiple nodes, analyzed using various Bivariate-Bicycle (BB) quantum error-correcting codes, such as [[18, 4, 4]] and [[54, 4, 8]].
key_observables: Logical Error Rate (LER) vs. Physical Error Rate (PER), and the comparison of LER for different fanout methods (1-shot GHZ vs. 3-CNOT sequence).
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), number of physical qubits ($n$), physical error rate ($p_{ebit}$), and the overhead associated with encoding 'upgrading' or caching.
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed for specific node configurations (e.g., 4-node setup) and relies on specific noise models (e.g., depolarizing noise).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of distributed operations (fanout) and the comparison of LER vs. PER across different encoding schemes and fanout methods. Tables provide quantitative data on LER measurements.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares different encoding choices for distributed fanout, analyzes the trade-off between code distance and resource overhead, and proposes architectural improvements like encoding upgrading and caching.
why_interesting: The findings provide concrete guidelines on resource optimization in large-scale quantum computation, showing that increasing code distance can be a more effective strategy than minimizing physical qubit count for maintaining low logical error rates.
